subjects.displayTitle: Love of country and the wider homeland
subjects.introduction: Because I live in this house, must I treat the man next door as a stranger? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s question exposes the oddity of lines drawn across a single continent, and Bahá’u’lláh goes further: glory belongs not to the one who loves his country but to the one who loves the world. Love of country is not condemned; Shoghi Effendi says a citizen serves his nation best by working, as a citizen of the world, for the federal principle among nations, and every country’s frontiers and independence deserve impartial protection. What is condemned is the point at which attachment turns into an owl’s devotion to a ruined wall, a gilded cage decorated by its own prisoners, or dogs howling over their corner of a public square, while the dust that is fought over is finally the dust of the grave. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá counts the cost in captive women, orphaned children and whole peoples displaced, and asks what consolation a bereaved child can find in a flag. Epictetus, reasoning from kinship with the divine to citizenship of the world, offers a different ground for the same enlargement of belonging [1]. The way forward passes through prejudice in all its forms, racial and class divisions among them, and through a candid look at the culture that calls such narrowness patriotism.
subjects.arc: Begin with familiar neighbors, enlarge the meaning of service to country, confront exclusion and its human costs, and move toward education and world community.

order.why: Open with the familiar relation between neighboring homes and extend it across borders.
Consider world citizenship as a way of serving one’s country.
Introduce the central call to love the world.
Place international protection of frontiers beside that wider loyalty.
Affirm the desire of each nation for freedom and self-determination.
Examine how a bond within one nation can become an obstacle between nations.
shortened: Another unifying force is patriotism. This too prevents unity and agreement between nations and parties, since the people of each country put their own homeland first. The French say all countries should be under our homeland. Similarly, out of love for homeland, each establishes privileges for their own country and wants others to be conquered and subjugated.

order.why: Expose the contradiction of prosperity sought through another people’s subjection.
shortened: Although this aspiration and thought is beneficial for themselves, their family, and indeed all their fellow citizens and countrymen, it is detrimental to other nations. For they strive with all their might to direct all the benefits of humanity toward their own nation, all the bounties of the earth to their own family, and all the happiness of the human world to themselves. They consider that the decline of other nations and neighboring powers leads to the advancement of their own nation and country, so that through this means they might achieve supremacy and dominance over others in power, wealth and authority.

order.why: Give that confinement a memorable image: the gilded cage.
Follow with the story of attachment to a ruined dwelling.
Question territorial rivalry through the stark image of the grave.
Deepen the reflection on soil, mortality, and the price of conflict.
Set national rivalries against the scale of the earth and cosmos.
shortened: Consider how unwise and short-sighted are the leaders, the politicians and the philosophers of the present age! The American continent and Europe, that is, Germany and France, are a small portion of the terrestrial globe. What is the importance of this globe?-for it commands no importance when compared to these infinite bodies that abound in the limitless space; it is like unto an insignificant spot on the surface of the wide ocean. No importance should be attached to the terrestrial globe, how much less to one of the countries of the globe.

order.why: Hear the critique in the setting of European patriotic fervor.
Read the longer wartime illustration of imagined partitions.
shortened: These countries over which you are so vociferous and at every moment show the signs of obstreperousness, are One Country, the home of humanity. Wherever man chooses to live, there is his home and his country. God has not divided this earth. It is one globe, one sphere. These boundaries that you have defined are the greatest illusions that man could ever conceive in his mind. They have no reality. It is similar to the division of one room into different sections, with so many hypothetical lines, calling this corner Germany, that corner France and another corner England.

order.why: Connect human nature with the possibility of peaceful association.
Move from geographical possession to the homeland of the heart.
shortened: I tell you what is required for conveying the message: Close your eyes to regional imaginings and worship of borders and territory and open them to the divine Kingdom. The homeland of humanity is pure hearts, not water and soil.

order.why: Make the critique concrete in the loss caused by attachment to dust.
Examine patriotism when it becomes a pretext for hatred.
Attend to the women, children, and displaced people affected by war.
Pause over a bereaved child and the search for consolation.
shortened: How difficult indeed is for those souls who are left behind to comfort themselves. Are the Kings and the emperors their comforters? Can they console themselves because they have shed their blood for their taskmasters, or for a piece of earth they have been led to believe as their 'country', the defence of which is 'patriotic'? Those who are left behind are sadly disillusioned but there will be neither hope nor courage to go on with their work while they are surrounded with so much misery. If they had shed their blood for a 'very great Cause', it would at least console their remnants; but now it is all for greed, selfishness, national pride, commercial motives etc.

order.why: Contrast the encounter of strangers in battle with service through light.
Read the reported assessment of patriotic unity in its historical setting.
Consider the reported pyramids illustration as a criticism of pride in domination.
Distinguish limited centers of unity from a universal center.
shortened: One of the "Collective Centers" has been and is yet considered the "spirit of nationalism."
Another "Collective Center" is "patriotism" the watchword and the battle-cry of the present nations. A third "Collective Center" is politics.

It is evident that the interest of one nation is the loss to another and we can see that as long as these three "Collective Centers" are dominant in the affairs of the world Universal Peace will not be realized. These "nations" look upon each other with the eyes of difference, they try to improve the conditions of their native countries at the expense of others and their interests clash and come within the range of conflict. Therefore all these "Collective Centers" instead of helping the cause of international Peace prevent its realization.

Consequently in this illumined century, the intellectual evolution of humanity has advanced far enough as to create a "Universal Collective Center" around which all the nations may revolve, thus sacrificing their petty interests for the progress of the whole.

order.why: Explore education and cultural encounter as means of widening sympathy.
Turn the removal of prejudice into a practical invitation to friendship.
Return to love of humankind after considering its obstacles.
shortened: One should not pride oneself on loving one's country, but rather should pride oneself on loving humankind.

order.why: Let the concise world-embracing call gather the argument.
Revisit the same standard of glory from another preserved selection.
Identifies patriotic, racial, religious and political prejudices as destructive barriers to human tranquility.
Connect the one-country image with the unity of humankind.
Complete the linked readings with the renewed call to love the world.
shortened: This is why in most Tablets this firm decree hath been sent down from the heaven of Will: "Glory is not for him who loveth his country, but for him who loveth the world."

order.why: Consider the additional reported criticism of human-made divisions.
shortened: This earth is one sphere. These geographical boundaries are made by man, calling one piece of land Austria, another Germany, a third French, a Fourth English and so forth. The dogs in Oriental cities instinctively divide the various quarters amongst themselves and if by chance one of the dogs crosses the boundary of another he will be attacked. But these boundary lines are all imaginary. They have no real existence."

order.why: Extend the comparison to cities receiving the same divine grace.
Reaffirm universal love in the additional supplied selection.
Revisit the limited unifying power of patriotism alongside religious fellowship.
shortened: Now, at times this unifying force is patriotism. Being fellow citizens is indeed a unifying force. However, this applies only to general benefits and harms and the attraction of common good; it has no authority in specific matters and no power over individuals.

Among all these, what truly serves as the unifying force of human society is religion. It unites different religions, unifies different nations, brings together different races, unites different languages, and unifies different homelands.

order.why: Ask what interdependence requires beyond nationally bounded institutions.
Close with the enlargement of social organization toward a world community.

questions: How might care for one’s country become more effective when its well-being is understood in relation to the whole world?
How can the passages criticizing territorial prejudice be read together with those affirming national freedom and secure frontiers?
What do the images of neighbors, a gilded cage, and a grave reveal about the attachments that shape us?
What do Epictetus and these selections each offer as a foundation for belonging beyond one’s birthplace?
How could education and cultural encounter help people recognize the human costs hidden by patriotic language?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the connection between service to country and world citizenship.
Consider a binding agreement that combines defined frontiers with collective security.
Read the analogy between human development and wider social organization.

references.label: 1 · Epictetus, Discourses I.9 (George Long translation)
references.note: In the opening paragraph, Epictetus moves from local ancestry to a community embracing humanity and the divine, and draws consequences for courage and belonging. Compare this spiritual basis for world citizenship with the compilation’s movement from love of country to responsibility for humankind. Consider how the Bahá’í selections carry the inquiry into education and institutions, beyond the individual’s understanding of identity.

subjects.introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá once watched a parliament descend from quibbling into a physical brawl, and drew the lesson that an assembly exists to reach the light of truth on the questions before it, not to serve as a battleground for self-opinion. Noise and clamour, He observed of Iran’s early parliaments, are not the same as investigating a people’s welfare. Constitutional government, He taught, is a religious principle and the requirement of the age; absolutism is illegitimate, and no nation prospers until its government and people are blended like honey and milk. But the form is not enough. Elected members must be righteous, incorruptible, learned in law and the arts of civilization, and content with their lawful pay, and each must come to see himself as a trustee of all humankind. Burke, telling the electors of Bristol that a member owes them his judgment and not merely his obedience, argues over the same ground of communication, independence and responsibility for the whole [1]. From national assemblies the vision widens to a supreme tribunal elected through the parliaments of the world, and then to a commonwealth that protects the autonomy of its members, distinct in its stages and from the institutions of the Faith itself. The journey continues into the relationship between government and people, the meaning of elections, and the long work of political unity.
subjects.arc: Begin with the quality of deliberation, examine constitutional responsibility in historical settings, then distinguish the institutions and stages of a wider order.

order.why: Open with the difference between discovering truth and winning an argument.
Test parliamentary activity against the welfare it should serve.
Introduce representation through public choice and responsibility.
Connect constitutional government with justice throughout society.
shortened: In the religion of God Constitutional government is a religious and binding principle. Every nation must diligently walk in this path and form a government of justice and fairness towards all the individuals of society.

order.why: Consider equal religious rights in the reported appeal for constitutional reform.
Read the affirmation of constitutional government in its Iranian setting.
shortened: We hope that constitutional government, which is the decisive text of the Most Holy Book, will be established in Iran and assurance will be obtained. Constitutional government, by the decisive text of the Most Holy Book, is legitimate government, while absolutism and autocracy are illegitimate.

order.why: Reflect on institutions responding to the needs of their time.
shortened: I wrote to him that the answer is ready, and it is this: "For every cycle there are certain exigencies. One cannot resist the exigency of the time. The time now requires that there should be a constitution, and not despotism, which latter is now impossible.
In the Book of Laws there is an evident text concerning the constitution, for a constitution is according to the law.

order.why: Place constitutional change within the passage’s historical comparisons.
Connect legitimate government with cooperation between people and authorities.
Make the need for cooperation vivid through the image of honey and milk.
Consider support for constitutional ideals in the specific Persian context.
Read the reported wartime contrast between autocracy and democracy.
Extend deliberation from a country to representatives of nations.
shortened: What he has accomplished in making treaties with various nations is very good, but when we have the interparliamentary body composed of delegates from all the nations of the world and devoted to the maintenance of agreement and goodwill, the utopian dream of sages and poets, the parliament of man, will be realized.

order.why: Describes parliamentary analogy and successive elections in forming a Supreme House of Justice.
Introduce the prospect of a world parliament and common law.
Begin the additional selections with the promise and conditions of parliamentary reform.
shortened: While the setting up of parliaments, the organizing of assemblies of consultation, constitutes the very foundation and bedrock of government, there are several essential requirements which these institutions must fulfill. First, the elected members must be righteous, God-fearing, high-minded, incorruptible. Second, they must be fully cognizant, in every particular, of the laws of God, informed as to the highest principles of law, versed in the rules which govern the management of internal affairs and the conduct of foreign relations, skilled in the useful arts of civilization, and content with their lawful emoluments.

order.why: Enlarge a representative’s trust to the welfare of all humankind.
Examine the historical discussion of constitutional monarchy and ministerial responsibility.
shortened: The mighty government and the brilliant nation should unite and establish a constitutional government, for the contingent world requires it, and one cannot prevent the requirements of existence. Every age has its requirements, and today's requirement is that governments be constitutional, as this brings comfort to the world of creation.

What could be better than having the national assembly and cabinet of ministers take responsibility for all affairs, accept accountability, serve the government, while the king, like the Emperor of England, lives in perfect comfort, security and happiness, with the entire nation devoted to him. Therefore, constitutionalism is preferable, but utmost caution must be exercised so it does not become like other cases.

order.why: Notice the proposed manner of addressing a ruler during reform.
Place the historical comparison with Wilson’s proposals beside those aspirations.
shortened: In brief, it hath become apparent to all that the spirit of the age and the well-being of this century are today dependent upon the Teachings revealed by the Pen of Glory. Even the President established fourteen points as the foundation of the League of Nations.1 Twelve of these were, fifty years ago, explicitly revealed by the Pen of the Most High, were disseminated throughout the world by means of newspapers and epistles, and the prominent people of Europe and America were apprised thereof.

order.why: Ask why existing international arrangements were judged insufficient to prevent war.
shortened: The meeting at The Hague should have such power and influence that its word will have an effect on the governments and nations. Point out to the revered members gathered there that the Hague Conference held before the war had as its President the Emperor of Russia, and its members were men of the greatest eminence. Nevertheless this did not prevent such a terrible war. Now how will it be? For in the future another war, fiercer than the last, will assuredly break out; verily, of this there is no doubt whatever. What can the Hague meeting do?

order.why: Consider a representative process for establishing a supreme tribunal.
shortened: And His plan is this: that the national assemblies of each country and nation--that is to say parliaments--should elect two or three persons who are the choicest of that nation, and are well informed concerning international laws and the relations between governments and aware of the essential needs of the world of humanity in this day. The number of these representatives should be in proportion to the number of inhabitants of that country. The election of these souls who are chosen by the national assembly, that is, the parliament, must be confirmed by the upper house, the congress and the cabinet and also by the president or monarch so these persons may be the elected ones of all the nation and the government. The Supreme Tribunal will be composed of these people, and all mankind will thus have a share therein, for every one of these delegates is fully representative of his nation.

order.why: Explore the proposed distribution of international legislative, executive, and judicial power.
Read the fuller vision of a commonwealth protecting diversity and autonomy.
shortened: The unity of the human race, as envisaged by Baha'u'llah, implies the establishment of a world commonwealth in which all nations, races, creeds and classes are closely and permanently united, and in which the autonomy of its state members and the personal freedom and initiative of the individuals that compose them are definitely and completely safeguarded. This commonwealth must, as far as we can visualize it, consist of a world legislature, whose members will, as the trustees of the whole of mankind, ultimately control the entire resources of all the component nations, and will enact such laws as shall be required to regulate the life, satisfy the needs and adjust the relationships of all races and peoples.

order.why: Distinguish a world government from the institutions of the Bahá’í Faith.
Make explicit the distinction between stages of world order.
shortened: The letters of Shoghi Effendi outline two stages in the development of world government. The first stage in this evolution is the emergence of "a world superstate" which will be associated with the establishment of the Lesser Peace.

The "World Parliament" referred to in "The Promise of World Peace" is an institution associated with this "superstate". In relation to the Lesser Peace, it is interesting to note that Shoghi Effendi, in a letter dated 14 Mar. 1939 written on his behalf, indicated that it "will come about through the political efforts of the states and nations of the world, and independently of any direct Baha'i plan or effort".

order.why: Trace the movement from political peace toward fuller spiritual and social unity.
shortened: We know, however, that peace will come in stages. First, there will come the Lesser Peace, when the unity of nations will be achieved, then gradually the Most Great Peace -- the spiritual as well as social and political unity of mankind, when the Baha'i World Commonwealth, operating in strict accordance with the laws and ordinances of the Most Holy Book of the Baha'i Revelation, will have been established through the efforts of the Baha'is.

order.why: Examine why the Bahá’í Administrative Order is not described as purely democratic.
Consider the anticipated development of elected Bahá’í institutions.
Read the supplied account of the Universal House of Justice within that framework.
Consider the longer development from religion to commonwealth.
Place recognition and institutional growth within the stated sequence of stages.
Close with the challenge of building amid social disintegration.

questions: What makes deliberation a search for truth, and what habits can turn it into a struggle for victory?
How should a representative hold together public wishes, informed judgment, and responsibility for people outside the constituency?
What becomes clearer when Burke’s account of representation is compared with the call to regard oneself as a trustee of humankind?
How do national parliaments, international institutions, and Bahá’í institutions differ in the passages, and why do those distinctions matter?
What capacities would citizens and representatives need for international decisions to earn durable trust?

neighbors.invitation: Consider public instruction as a foundation of collective life.
Explore the relationship between conscience, consultation, and institutional restraint.
Read the account of political peace developing through stages.

references.label: 1 · Edmund Burke, Speech to the Electors of Bristol, 3 November 1774
references.note: In the concluding discussion of instructions from constituents, Burke joins close communication with independent judgment and responsibility for the whole nation. Compare his reasoning with the selections on consultation and the wider trusteeship of representatives. His speech addresses a particular parliamentary constitution; it does not supply a model for identifying the authority or structure of Bahá’í institutions.

subjects.displayTitle: Political unity: making a common world possible
subjects.introduction: Warships refitted as merchant steamers, carrying goods between the nations they were built to bombard: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá offered that picture a century ago, and it still measures how far political life has to travel. The unity of governments is not a treaty signed by weary rulers but a change in the relationships that hold a society together. Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá return again and again to the bond between a government and its people, which must mingle like honey and milk if either is to prosper, to the schooling of a whole population, and to the freedom that universal peace is meant to secure. Nationality becomes a name rather than a wall. Kant, wondering how a league of peace could endure while states kept their liberty, posed a question the Bahá’í writings answer with a world commonwealth whose member states remain autonomous and whose citizens remain free [1]. Shoghi Effendi describes its institutions plainly: a world legislature, an executive, a supreme tribunal with binding verdicts. From here the journey runs through constitutional and parliamentary government, the stages from the Lesser Peace to the Most Great Peace, and the larger promise of world unity.
subjects.arc: Open with a peaceful use for instruments of war, connect global interdependence with domestic trust, and move toward representative international arrangements and a wider commonwealth.

order.why: Imagine national names within an overriding human fellowship.
shortened: Germany, France, England, Turkey, Arabia -- all these various nations will be welded together in unity. When the people of the future are asked, "To which nationality do you belong?" the answer will be, "To the nationality of humanity. I am living under the shadow of Baha'u'llah. I am the servant of Baha'u'llah. I belong to the army of the Most Great Peace." The people of the future will not say, "I belong to the nation of England, France or Persia"; for all of them will be citizens of a universal nationality -- the one family, the one country, the one world of humanity -- and then these wars, hatreds and strifes will pass away.

order.why: Open with the striking conversion of warships into vessels of commerce.
Show why interdependent problems call for a wider framework of law.
Connect service to one’s country with citizenship of the world.
Keep the suffering of families visible beneath the language of international order.
Define the ruler’s duty through peace and the freedom of peoples.
Introduce public instruction as a responsibility of the state.
Bring the inquiry home to cooperation between government and people.
Connects political unity and a supreme tribunal with the growth of public commitment to peace.
Use the image of honey and milk to describe that relationship.
shortened: Now again it is written that if the government and nation mix like honey and milk and conduct themselves with unity and accord, then well and good; otherwise the great calamity shall come.

order.why: Revisit the same image in a further preserved report.
Distinguish outward calm from underlying social division.
shortened: As to the situation in Iran, it hath not yet found tranquility. Though outwardly calm, inwardly it is turbulent, and this turbulence stems from lack of unity and agreement of views. It was written from beginning to end that government and people must blend together like honey and milk, otherwise it is certain that the result of opposition is deadly poison and gives rise to hatred and rancor.

order.why: Consider the body and its arteries as an image of mutual dependence.
Connect stable government with the reconciliation of divided groups.
shortened: It is incumbent upon the divine friends to unite the hearts of the nation, so that different parties may become one party, and so that through the unity and agreement of the nation every just government may gain strength and stability and become the cause of Iran's comfort and tranquility.

order.why: Read the juxtaposition of one earthly home and religion’s relation to politics.
Explore the Covenant’s role in safeguarding a spiritual community’s unity.
shortened: Then by Thy Supreme Pen Thou didst write the Book of the Covenant and inscribe the Tablet of the Testament, so that no room would remain for doubt or misgiving, and the Cause and Center of God's Cause would be as clear as the sun, and no one could create a breach or cast into Thy blessed Cause - which is the greatest means of unifying the world and removing differences between nations - the odor of discord and dissension, destroying this mighty edifice and turning this Most Glorious Paradise into a thorny wilderness.

order.why: Consider religious fellowship as a historical source of wider association.
shortened: For example, Christ, alone and single-handedly, raised the banner of peace and amity--a feat that the combined forces of all the mighty governments of the world are unable to accomplish. Consider how numerous are the diverse governments and peoples--such as Italy, France, Germany, Russia, England, and the like--who have been gathered together under the same canopy!

order.why: Bring religious unity into the inquiry about human unity.
Join universal peace with religious fellowship and prosperity.
Read the invitation to association across East and West.
shortened: If this association acts with independence and strives for the connection of East and West, it is among the principles of the unity of the human world if it becomes established, for minor affairs do not progress without firmness and steadfastness, let alone such great matters.

order.why: Consider the reported call for mutual sacrifice between peoples.
Preserve the specific historical hope for friendship while considering its wider principle.
Pause over the hope for lasting amicable relations.
shortened: Our hope is that their differences will be settled soon and amicable relations based on a sound permanent basis be established.

order.why: Reaffirm peace among governments and nations as a purpose of the Cause.
Recognize service through the contemporary peace conference addressed in the passage.
shortened: Now, since the League of Nations Conference established in London is among the branches of the unity of the human world, we therefore remember you with utmost respect that, praise be to God, you have arisen for this universal service, and God willing, day by day that assembly will expand and become the cause of achieving general benefits and universal fellowship and love between the nations of the world.

order.why: Examine the relation between international conference and spiritual influence.
Read the response to reports of leaders seeking peace.
Hear the public aspiration for peace gathering strength.
shortened: The Cry of Peace is being heard from every throat and the sweet, resonant harmony of Peace shall drown all the screeching noises of war. Blessed are those who are enlisted in the rank of Peace!

order.why: Consider the historical hope for an American contribution to agreement.
shortened: May this American democracy be the first nation to establish the foundation of international agreement. May it be the first nation to proclaim the universality of mankind. May it be the first to upraise the standard of the Most Great Peace, and through this nation of democracy may these philanthropic intentions and institutions be spread broadcast throughout the world.

order.why: Revisit that invitation as a responsibility to assist others.
Examine the reported limitations of an early international council’s representation.
Ask what new relationships require of international ethics and law.
Complete the linked readings with the need for a comprehensive plan.
shortened: Today the distinguished leaders of nations must sing such a song in the ears of the people that the heart of the world of humanity may be stirred into cheerfulness, and draft such a comprehensive plan of universal union that its reflection may be cast upon the mirror of the world of existence and be none other than the real prototype and portrait of the Realm on High.

order.why: Begin the additional selections with goodwill toward both government and people.
Return to the dangers of their division in the Iranian setting.
Read the supplied constitutional telegram passage alongside that danger.
shortened: O herald of the Covenant! Your letter arrived and its contents were understood. When you were at the Holy Shrine, the matter of government officials and the people was explained to you in detail explicitly. Surely you have mentioned this in the spiritual gathering. According to recent telegrams, good news of unity between government and people has arrived. His Majesty has ordered the implementation of constitutional government. Praise be to God, everything written in 'Abdu'l-Baha's letters is being manifested successively in its entirety.

order.why: Consider the federal illustration of a wider union.
Explore the reported extension of that illustration to autonomous European states.
shortened: If there has been possible in the past the formation of a United States of America, the next natural step will be the constitution of a United States of Europe, each state autonomous within its boundary, interdependent and working for the common prosperity, general advancement, expansion of commerce, diffusion of learning, the welfare of the whole communit[y], the socialization of industries and the improvement of arts, inventions, crafts and sciences.

order.why: Consider the proposed continuing congress of thinkers and statesmen.
shortened: Considering carefully these important facts, it behooveth you, from amongst the rulers of the earth, to unfurl the Flag of Universal Peace in the land of the ancient Pharaohs. You can render this priceless service to your country and the world at large by calling together an International Congress of Universal Peace to be held annually in Egypt and invite to it hundreds of the world's foremost thinkers, scholars, philosophers and statesmen - in brief a Parliamen[t] of the world of humanity, a symposia of the East and the West, the North and the South.

order.why: Place the peace aspiration within the history recalled by the selection.
Ask why limited collective centers cannot embrace the whole world.
shortened: In the matter of universal Peace, a great universal Power is necessary, what we may name a "Universal Collective Center." In the past there have appeared several "Collective Centers." These "Collective Centers" not being general in their various aspects have given only limited results.
Therefore all these "Collective Centers" instead of helping the cause of international Peace prevent its realization.

Consequently in this illumined century, the intellectual evolution of humanity has advanced far enough as to create a "Universal Collective Center" around which all the nations may revolve, thus sacrificing their petty interests for the progress of the whole.

order.why: Read the fifth candle’s historical formulation of unity of nations.
shortened: The fourth candle is unity in religion which is the corner-stone of the foundation itself, and which, by the power of God, will be revealed in all its splendour. The fifth candle is the unity of nations -- a unity which in this century will be securely established, causing all the peoples of the world to regard themselves as citizens of one common fatherland.

order.why: Examine the fuller commonwealth vision, including the freedom of its component peoples.
shortened: The unity of the human race, as envisaged by Baha'u'llah, implies the establishment of a world commonwealth in which all nations, races, creeds and classes are closely and permanently united, and in which the autonomy of its state members and the personal freedom and initiative of the individuals that compose them are definitely and completely safeguarded. This commonwealth must, as far as we can visualize it, consist of a world legislature, whose members will, as the trustees of the whole of mankind, ultimately control the entire resources of all the component nations, and will enact such laws as shall be required to regulate the life, satisfy the needs and adjust the relationships of all races and peoples. A world executive, backed by an international Force, will carry out the decisions arrived at, and apply the laws enacted by, this world legislature, and will safeguard the organic unity of the whole commonwealth. A world tribunal will adjudicate and deliver its compulsory and final verdict in all and any disputes that may arise between the various elements constituting this universal system.

order.why: Close by connecting political transformation with collective maturity.
shortened: ...the Guardian has already advised you to stress in your talks the idea of a world superstate, and the concept of the Oneness of Mankind underlying it. In addition, he wishes you also to emphasize the fact that humanity, taken as a whole, has entered the most critical and momentous stage of its evolution, the stage of maturity. This idea of the coming of age of mankind constitutes the central core of the Baha'i Teachings, and is the most distinguishing feature of the Revelation of Baha'u'llah.

questions: What changes when peace is imagined through schools, trust, trade, and public law as well as through agreements among rulers?
How might unity between government and people be cultivated without suppressing honest disagreement?
Where do the readings place the boundary between necessary common authority and the autonomy of nations and individuals?
How does Kant’s federation illuminate the strengths and limits of different forms of international agreement?
How might the relationships practiced in a local community prepare people to participate responsibly in a wider political world?

neighbors.invitation: Examine a national bond that unites some people while separating them from others.
Consider the habits that make common deliberation fruitful.
Distinguish political unity from a fuller spiritual and social peace.

references.label: 1 · Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace, Second Definitive Article
references.note: Kant distinguishes a lasting league of peace from a treaty ending a particular war. He considers a world republic, then discusses a growing federation in light of states’ unwillingness to accept wider compulsion. Compare that tension between freedom and common law with the compilation’s account of a world commonwealth. The comparison invites attention to institutional differences as well as a shared aspiration to enduring peace.

subjects.displayTitle: The stages of peace: agreement and transformation
subjects.introduction: Count what an army costs, and then picture the same treasure and the same inventive minds turned toward the general well-being: that is how ‘Abdu’l-Bahá makes peace concrete before He makes it spiritual. Bahá’u’lláh addresses the rulers of the earth with a sober offer. Having turned away from the Most Great Peace, let them at least hold fast to the Lesser Peace: be reconciled, reduce armaments to what security requires, meet in a vast assemblage, and bind themselves to rise together against any king who takes up arms. That political settlement has real worth, and it will pass through stages and great upheavals before it is won. Beyond it lies a fuller peace in which tyranny becomes justice and poverty becomes wealth, a transformation that human powers alone cannot produce. Isaiah’s vision of nations seeking instruction and beating their swords into ploughshares sets learning, judgment and disarmament in the same sequence [1]. The road continues through the unity of governments and political unity, through the long question of war and peace, and toward the world unity that gives each partial achievement its meaning.
subjects.arc: Begin with the human benefit of disarmament, develop the means of collective security, and distinguish practical stages from the fuller transformation they prepare.

order.why: Introduce the explicit distinction between the rejected Most Great Peace and the call for the Lesser Peace.
Open with the redirection of inventive ability and resources toward well-being.
shortened: In the first place, therefore, the servants of God--that is to say, all the inhabitants of a state--would be freed from bearing the burden of the tremendous expense of an army; in the second, the many persons who now devote their lives to the invention of fresh instruments of war would no longer waste their time on such work, which but encourages ferocity and bloodthirstiness, and is repugnant to the universal ideal of humanity. On the contrary, they would employ their natural gifts in the cause if the general well-being and would contribute towards the peace and salvation of mankind.

order.why: Consider the proposed assembly of rulers and binding collective security.
shortened: The Great Being, wishing to reveal the prerequisites of the peace and tranquillity of the world and the advancement of its peoples, hath written:  The time must come when the imperative necessity for the holding of a vast, an all-embracing assemblage of men will be universally realized.  The rulers and kings of the earth must needs attend it, and, participating in its deliberations, must consider such ways and means as will lay the foundations of the world's Great Peace amongst men.  Such a peace demandeth that the Great Powers should resolve, for the sake of the tranquillity of the peoples of the earth, to be fully reconciled among themselves.  Should any king take up arms against another, all should unitedly arise and prevent him.  If this be done, the nations of the world will no longer require any armaments, except for the purpose of preserving the security of their realms and of maintaining internal order within their territories.

order.why: Read the detailed requirements of an internationally sanctioned agreement.
shortened: True civilization will unfurl its banner in the midmost heart of the world whenever a certain number of its distinguished and high-minded sovereigns -- the shining exemplars of devotion and determination -- shall, for the good and happiness of all mankind, arise, with firm resolve and clear vision, to establish the Cause of Universal Peace. They must make the Cause of Peace the object of general consultation, and seek by every means in their power to establish a Union of the nations of the world. They must conclude a binding treaty and establish a covenant, the provisions of which shall be sound, inviolable and definite. They must proclaim it to all the world and obtain for it the sanction of all the human race.

order.why: Connect reconciliation and reduced armaments with relief from public expense.
Examine why disarmament must be concerted among nations.
shortened: Now the question of disarmament must be put into practice by all the nations and not only by one or two.

order.why: Read the reported proposal for concurrent disarmament in its historical setting.
Consider the responsibilities assigned to public authorities in promoting peace.
Receive the Lesser Peace as a glad-tiding.
Place moderation and unity beside the destructive possibilities of civilization.
Widen the horizon to the transformation of tyranny and poverty.
Consider cooperation and equality as foundations of common action.
shortened: It will reach such a degree that all conventions of the world will become humble and submissive before this Convention, for its foundation is the unity of the human world, universal peace, fellowship and love between all humanity, cooperation and equality between all nations, and the dawning of the light of truth.

order.why: Recognize the work of a peace society and its shared aspiration.
Reaffirm peace as a central teaching and desire.
Turn the aspiration into a personal invitation to serve.
shortened: Become the instrument of the Most Great Peace for all people and promote reconciliation between East and West.

order.why: Imagine the joy associated with assemblies serving human oneness.
shortened: It must be established so that the world of creation may find rest, and East and West and the five continents of the world may embrace one another, and all may repose beneath the pavilion of the unity of humankind, until the banner of universal peace waves over all horizons. Until this issue becomes the light of the world's assemblies, eternal happiness will not be attained and estrangement will not be transformed into unity.

order.why: Read the historical hope for an American contribution.
Move from conflict toward reconciliation in relationships.
shortened: Strife and conflict will surely be removed from all the nations of the earth. Carnage shall be taken away; fighting, violence and reviling will be changed into universal reconciliation and the hosts of tranquillity will pitch their tents in the midst of the world.

order.why: Consider the hope for the Most Great Peace in the reported passage.
Connects peace, the order of the world and the progress of nations with consultation among rulers.
Let prayer express the spiritual horizon of that hope.
shortened: O God! Raise aloft the banner of the oneness of mankind and establish the Most Great Peace.

order.why: Complete the linked readings by acknowledging the upheavals foreseen along the way.
Consider service to peace as a measure of beneficent action.
shortened: Today the greatest service to the Kingdom of God is promoting human unity and serving universal peace.
They are the cause of death while you are the cause of life.
And among the greatest teachings of Baha'u'llah is universal peace which is the cause of comfort and tranquility for humanity.
Today the greatest foundation of the Kingdom of God is promoting universal peace and the unity of the human world.

order.why: Read the reported link between awakening and a tribunal.
Confront self-interest as an obstacle within peace negotiations.
shortened: Although the representatives of governments have assembled in Paris to establish the foundation of universal peace and bestow comfort and tranquility upon the human world, yet misunderstanding still prevails and self-interest remains. Therefore, universal peace will not easily manifest and new difficulties will arise, for intentions are not in harmony - rather, desires are different. We must supplicate and implore the Kingdom of God and seek comfort and tranquility for the human world, for the Most Great Peace cannot be realized through human powers and will not manifest in the realm of existence.

order.why: Pause over the transition from the dawn of peace to the sun of affection.
Attend to the stated limits of knowledge about institutional relationships and dates.
Examine the Lesser Peace as a process with stages and continuing opportunities for service.
shortened: As to the Lesser Peace, Shoghi Effendi has explained that this will initially be a political unity arrived at by decision of the governments of various nations; it will not be established by direct action of the Baha'i community. This does not mean, however, that the Baha'is are standing aside and waiting for the Lesser Peace to come before they do something about the peace of mankind.

The Lesser Peace itself will pass through stages; at the initial stage the governments will act entirely on their own without the conscious involvement of the Faith; later on, in God's good time, the Faith will have a direct influence on it in ways indicated by Shoghi Effendi in his "The Goal of a New World Order."

order.why: Distinguish political agreement from a peace grounded in Bahá’í institutions and law.
Read the fuller explanation of spiritual, social, and political unity.
shortened: We know, however, that peace will come in stages. First, there will come the Lesser Peace, when the unity of nations will be achieved, then gradually the Most Great Peace -- the spiritual as well as social and political unity of mankind, when the Baha'i World Commonwealth, operating in strict accordance with the laws and ordinances of the Most Holy Book of the Baha'i Revelation, will have been established through the efforts of the Baha'is.

order.why: Consider the limits assigned to political machinery alone.
Preserve the historically addressed encouragement to youth within its own setting.
Close with the education and reconstruction required by the oneness of humanity.
shortened: Acceptance of the oneness of mankind is the first fundamental prerequisite for reorganization and administration of the world as one country, the home of humankind. Universal acceptance of this spiritual principle is essential to any successful attempt to establish world peace. It should therefore be universally proclaimed, taught in schools, and constantly asserted in every nation as preparation for the organic change in the structure of society which it implies. In the Baha'i view, recognition of the oneness of mankind "calls for no less than the reconstruction and the demilitarization of the whole civilized world -- a world organically unified in all the essential aspects of its life, its political machinery, its spiritual aspiration, its trade and finance, its script and language, and yet infinite in the diversity of the national characteristics of its federated units."

questions: What benefits make a political peace worth working for even while deeper sources of conflict remain?
How do common agreement, collective enforcement, and the education of peoples support one another?
What does Isaiah’s movement from instruction and judgment to peaceful cultivation bring into focus in these selections?
How can hope for future peace encourage patient action without turning uncertain details into a timetable?
What forms of service are open to individuals and communities during the different stages described?

neighbors.invitation: Begin with a concrete image of military resources serving peaceful exchange.
Explore the relationship between a promised future and human responsibility.
Read the distinction between political world unity and later institutional development.

references.label: 1 · Isaiah 2:2–4 (King James Version)
references.note: Isaiah pictures peoples seeking divine instruction, judgment among nations, and weapons remade for cultivation. Compare the connection among learning, justice, and disarmament with the practical and spiritual dimensions of peace in this compilation. The prophetic vision provides a fruitful comparison; it does not by itself define the Bahá’í distinction between the Lesser Peace and the Most Great Peace.

subjects.displayTitle: Humanity’s maturity: new capacities and responsibilities
subjects.introduction: Every created thing has its hour of ripeness, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes: the tree when it bears fruit, the plant when it flowers, the human being when the light of intelligence reaches its full power. The human race, He teaches, has passed through its childhood and its turbulent youth and now stands at the threshold of its own maturity, so that the arrangements adequate to an earlier age no longer fit. Shoghi Effendi calls this idea the central core of the teachings. Yet the same voices insist that maturity is not yet attained: the material civilization of the day must still be infused with a divine one, and the sign of its arrival is universal peace. Augustine, tracing humanity’s education through successive ages, offers a kindred image from another theology [1]. The journey from here leads into the oneness of humanity and world unity, toward the new race of men this age is meant to bring forth, and even into alchemy, whose elixir was promised to a world come of age.
subjects.arc: Begin with the experience of growing capacities, distinguish promise from realization, and explore the responsibilities and institutions of a collective coming of age.

order.why: Distinguish the ripening of potential from an end to further progress.
shortened: The world of humanity has, heretofore, been in the stage of infancy; now it is approaching maturity. Just as the individual human organism, having attained the period of maturity, reaches its fullest degree of physical strength and ripened intellectual faculties so that in one year of this ripened period there is witnessed an unprecedented measure of development, likewise the world of humanity in this cycle of its completeness and consummation will realize an immeasurable upward progress, and that power of accomplishment whereof each individual human reality is the depository of God -- that outworking Universal Spirit -- like the intellectual faculty, will reveal itself in infinite degrees of perfection.

order.why: Open with the accessible comparison between individual growth and changing collective needs. Return to organic growth through the images of fruit and bloom.
shortened: All created things have their degree, or stage, of maturity. The period of maturity in the life of a tree is the time of its fruit bearing. The maturity of a plant is the time of its blossoming and flower.

Similarly, there are periods and stages in the life of the aggregate world of humanity, which at one time was passing through its degree of childhood, at another its time of youth but now has entered its long presaged period of maturity, the evidences of which are everywhere visible and apparent. Therefore, the requirements and conditions of former periods have changed and merged into exigencies which distinctly characterize the present age of the world of mankind.

order.why: Develop the parallel through the emergence of human powers.
Explore awakening reason as a sign of a new stage.
shortened: Consider how a child arrives at maturity. Suddenly the light of intellect will shine upon him and man will then make extraordinary progress. It will be as though he were asleep but was awakened; as though he were heedless but became intelligent; as though he were blind but received his sight. Before arriving at maturity he knew nothing. When he reached maturity and the light of reason shone, then he discovered the realities of the things.

order.why: Make new requirements concrete through the image of changed food and appetite.
Consider the inadequacy of habits inherited from adolescence.
Read the qualification that material development alone has not brought maturity.
Compares humanity’s collective development with a child reaching maturity and capacity for spiritual understanding.
Attend carefully to the signs referred to in the Aqdas passage.
Consider the supplied discussion of peace, wisdom, and hidden capacities. Compare the additional provisional rendering of the passage on signs of maturity.
Complete the linked readings with the reported image of a new age of light.
Join reason and education with material and divine civilization.
shortened: When man reacheth the stage of maturity, the lights of reason shine forth, and the perfections of the human world become manifest. We may therefore say that all the progress which man hath made from the beginning hath been but the preliminary stages for the manifestation of this mighty reason.
Reason, in the world of man, is the most great thing.

order.why: Distinguish enduring principles from the requirements of a new stage.
shortened: In the coming of Christ, the divine teachings were given in accordance with the infancy of the human race. The teachings of Baha'u'llah have the same basic principles, but are according to the stage of the maturity of the world and the requirements of this illumined age. O thou seeker of the Kingdom! Make thou an effort so that thou mayest partake from the spiritual Supper of the Lord.

order.why: Read the relationship between successive divine educators and humanity’s development.
shortened: Convey my spiritual greetings to the handmaiden of God, Sungamitta, and say to her that each of the Manifestations in previous Dispensations had a station in existence and a rank in human development. But the Manifestation of the Most Great Name--may my spirit be a sacrifice for His loved ones--represents the maturity and coming of age of human reality in the world of existence.

order.why: Read the supplied sign concerning the burden of kingship.
shortened: In one of the Tablets it was revealed that among the signs of the world's maturity is that no one will accept to bear alone the weight of kingship. Sovereignty will remain, but none will be willing to bear alone its burden. Those will be the days when wisdom will be manifest among mankind, save for him who may take on this mighty weight for the sake of propagating God's Cause and spreading His Faith.

order.why: Read the historical account of humanity passing through adolescence.
Examine the tension between turbulence and the prospect of wisdom.
Consider how recognizing immaturity could encourage the construction of peace.
Question the adequacy of models shaped by humanity’s adolescence.
Balance that critique with acknowledgment of earlier institutional achievements.
shortened: The great emphasis on the distinctiveness of the Order of Baha'u'llah is not meant to belittle existing systems of government. Indeed, they are to be recognized as the fruit of a vast period of social evolution, representing an advanced stage in the development of social organization. What motivates us is the knowledge that the supreme mission of the Revelation of Baha'u'llah, the Bearer of that Order, is, as Shoghi Effendi pointed out, "none other but the achievement of this organic and spiritual unity of the whole body of nations", indicating the "coming of age of the entire human race".

order.why: Bring maturity into individual conscience, consultation, and the limits of legislation.
shortened: There is also a clear pattern already established in the Sacred Scriptures, in the interpretations made by 'Abdu'l-Baha and Shoghi Effendi, and in the decisions so far made by the Universal House of Justice, whereby an area of the application of the laws is intentionally left to the conscience of each individual believer. This is the age in which mankind must attain maturity, and one aspect of this is the assumption by individuals of the responsibility for deciding, with the assistance of consultation, their own course of action in areas which are left open by the law of God.

order.why: Explore revelation as the source of a collective coming of age.
Consider the capacities attributed to the present revelation.
Connect collective maturity with the organization of human welfare.
Examine the disruption associated with newly released creative energies.
Locate the theme within the account of Bahá’u’lláh’s mission.
Keep the reported pilgrim-note reflection on discovery in its distinct source setting.
Consider the formative work assigned to the second century of the Faith.
Distinguish that work from the Golden Age still anticipated.
Revisit maturity as a central concept of the teachings.
shortened: In addition, he wishes you also to emphasize the fact that humanity, taken as a whole, has entered the most critical and momentous stage of its evolution, the stage of maturity. This idea of the coming of age of mankind constitutes the central core of the Baha'i Teachings, and is the most distinguishing feature of the Revelation of Baha'u'llah. A proper understanding of this concept gives the key to an adequate appreciation of the tremendous claim made by the Author of the Faith, both with regard to His own station, and to the incomparable greatness of His Dispensation.

order.why: Close with the possibility of conscious choice at a turning point in human affairs.

questions: What does the analogy of a growing person clarify about humanity’s development, and where might that analogy have limits?
How can passages announcing a coming of age be read alongside those describing maturity as still to be attained?
What should a maturing society preserve from earlier achievements, and what might it need to outgrow?
How do Augustine’s account of divine education and these selections differently describe the direction of humanity’s growth?
What would a more mature exercise of conscience, consultation, and responsibility look like in everyday collective life?

neighbors.invitation: Explore education as a responsibility supporting collective capacity.
Consider deliberation as a discipline of mature judgment.
Read about the prolonged rethinking of relationships required by human oneness.

references.label: 1 · Augustine, City of God, Book X, chapter 14 (Marcus Dods translation)
references.note: Chapter 14 compares the education of humanity, represented by the people of God, with an individual’s growth through successive ages. Its movement is from temporal and visible things toward eternal and invisible realities. The original compilation already points to this passage. Compare the use of developmental imagery while considering the distinctive Bahá’í emphasis here on the collective capacities and institutions of a united humanity.

subjects.displayTitle: Building civilization: the means and the people
subjects.introduction: Nations do not need war to outstrip one another, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes; there are thousands of praiseworthy ways to advance, from building cities and spreading education to promoting the sciences and arts, and none of them costs a drop of blood. The question then becomes what the actual means of a future civilization are. He names some plainly: armies reduced to a police of the seas so that their budgets can relieve poverty and fund learning, an auxiliary language that unlocks the box of the heart and lets knowledge travel, public opinion turned patiently toward arbitration, and beneath these a spiritual illumination that reshapes social forms from within. Confucius, asked what to do for a numerous people, answered enrich them, and then teach them, the same joining of provision and learning in a far older key [1]. The work spans generations, and delay has a price in human suffering. The road runs toward a universal language and universal peace, toward the spiritualisation of humanity that alone can sustain them, and toward the flowering of arts and sciences in a world made one.
subjects.arc: Begin with constructive uses of human ability, develop the social and spiritual means of progress, distinguish institutional principles, and return to participation and responsibility.

order.why: Bring spiritual illumination into the development of just social forms.
shortened: Among the results of the manifestation of spiritual forces will be that the human world will adapt itself to a new social form, the justice of God will become manifest throughout human affairs, and human equality will be universally established.

order.why: Open with constructive fields in which human energy and aspiration can flourish.
Connect reduced military expenditure with the relief of poverty and advancement of knowledge.
Consider a common language as a means of education and mutual understanding.
shortened: Therefore, the question of an auxiliary international tongue has the utmost importance. Through this means international education and training become possible; the evidence and history of the past can be acquired. The spread of the known facts of the human world depends upon language. The explanation of divine teachings can only be through this medium. As long as diversity of tongues and lack of comprehension of other languages continue, these glorious aims cannot be realized.

order.why: Join material and divine civilization in the image of a renewed springtime.
Examine the complementary responsibilities of law, learning, and government.
shortened: The state is, moreover, based upon two potent forces, the legislative and the executive. The focal center of the executive power is the government, while that of the legislative is the learned -- and if this latter great support and pillar should prove defective, how is it conceivable that the state should stand?

order.why: Place service to country within a wider federal community.
Consider public opinion moving toward arbitration under the cost of war.
shortened: The warring Powers having exhausted their resources will then enter into closer bond of intimacy and having destroyed the tree of militarism root and branch will be willing to listen to the voice of the pacifists of all countries; the cause of eternal peace will be strengthened; its advocates increased and the enlightened public opinion of mankind will demand the establishment of the International Court of Arbitration.

order.why: Ask what happens when agreement fails to keep pace with armament.
Explore the reported practical actions through which a public commitment to peace might spread.
shortened: Also, if these ideas regarding peace spread among the public, the financiers will refuse to give loans for wars and the manufacture of armaments, the railway companies will abstain from transporting instruments of destruction and the armed forces will not engage in carnage and the spilling of blood. Also the boundaries should be established.

order.why: Read the historical discussion of peaceful methods of reform.
Connect participation in peace societies with the passage’s emphasis on spiritual power.
Hear the reported appeal for unity after the long experience of conflict.
Consider the new plans and relationships called for after war.
shortened: After this war new plans, new thoughts and new sound theories are essential. Old thoughts will be good for the scrapbasket. A new table must be spread, new dishes must be cooked and new appetite must be cultivated. The seeds of new flowers must be sown, new saplings must be planted, new roads must be constructed, a new code of ethics must be discovered, new conventions for the amicable settlement of international disputes must be evolved, new lamps must be lighted, new truths must be laid here, new capability and ability must be trained, new modes of expression must be found, new worlds must be conquered, new relations must be established and new standards of life must be upraised.

order.why: Examine the relation between human will and divine guidance.
Connects the education of children in basic virtues with the foundations of future civilization and human solidarity.
Place practical reconstruction within the upheaval associated with a new world order.
Complete the linked readings with the image of a divine springtime.
shortened: This is the Paradise the rustling of whose leaves proclaimeth: "O ye that inhabit the heavens and the earth! There hath appeared what hath never previously appeared.

order.why: Connect selfless aims with a new pattern of life.
shortened: Amid the factions of the earth, this community of the Most Great Name standeth detached from every vain fancy, severed from every selfish aim, established in purity of motive, and striving and laboring with utmost longing in the divine teachings, that the face of the earth may become a very paradise, that the world of humanity may be transformed into a mirror of the Kingdom, that this world may become another world, and that the human race may acquire a new education, a new way, and a new manner of life.

order.why: Read the reported house-building image of institutional preparation.
Begin the additional selections with the transformation of heart, outlook, conduct, and environment.
Welcome effective methods that contribute to an advancing civilization.
Consider the long rethinking of relationships that follows recognition of oneness.
Explore why that recognition calls for new community and administrative arrangements.
Acknowledge earlier political achievements while considering organic change.
shortened: The great emphasis on the distinctiveness of the Order of Baha'u'llah is not meant to belittle existing systems of government. Indeed, they are to be recognized as the fruit of a vast period of social evolution, representing an advanced stage in the development of social organization.
In practical terms, His mission signals the advent of "an organic change in the structure of present-day society, a change such as the world has not yet experienced".

order.why: Examine peaceful and constructive reform as a matter of method.
Read the rejection of simple identification with existing political systems.
Consider the stated combination of beneficial elements within a distinct order.
Revisit that combination through the additional preserved explanation.
Read the fuller account of the Administrative Order’s distinctive character.
shortened: The Baha'i Commonwealth of the future, of which this vast Administrative Order is the sole framework, is, both in theory and practice, not only unique in the entire history of political institutions, but can find no parallel in the annals of any of the world's recognized religious systems.

This new-born Administrative Order incorporates within its structure certain elements which are to be found in each of the three recognized forms of secular government, without being in any sense a mere replica of any one of them, and without introducing within its machinery any of the objectionable features which they inherently possess....

order.why: Attend to the limits of institutional analogies and the particular sources of authority.
shortened: In emphasizing its distinctiveness, Shoghi Effendi has pointed out that "this Administrative Order is fundamentally different from anything that any Prophet has previously established, inasmuch as Baha'u'llah has Himself revealed its principles, established its institutions, appointed the person to interpret His Word and conferred the necessary authority on the body designed to supplement and apply His legislative ordinances". In another statement, he maintains that, "It would be utterly misleading to attempt a comparison between this unique, divinely-conceived Order and any of the diverse systems which the minds of men, at various periods of their history, have contrived for the government of human institutions."

order.why: Preserve the pilgrim-note discussion of economic organization within its source category.
Consider the role assigned to revealed institutions in preserving unity.
Trace the stated stages of the Faith’s institutional development.
Compare the longer historical account of those stages.
Widen the goal beyond immediate humanitarian benefits to the purpose of human life.
Connect confidence in the future with responsibility for delays and suffering.
Consider the choice between suffering and consultative action in humanity’s approach to peace.
shortened: The Great Peace towards which people of good will throughout the centuries have inclined their hearts, of which seers and poets for countless generations have expressed their vision, and for which from age to age the sacred scriptures of mankind have constantly held the promise, is now at long last within the reach of the nations. For the first time in history it is possible for everyone to view the entire planet, with all its myriad diversified peoples, in one perspective. World peace is not only possible but inevitable. It is the next stage in the evolution of this planet -- in the words of one great thinker, "the planetization of mankind".* Whether peace is to be reached only after unimaginable horrors precipitated by humanity's stubborn clinging to old patterns of behaviour, or is to be embraced now by an act of consultative will, is the choice before all who inhabit the earth.

order.why: Bring participation within reach of people with limited means.
Read a historically specific plan as an example of organized capacity-building.
Return to the urgency and privilege of present service.
Set present work within the selection’s long spiritual horizon.
Close with the fuller vision of a civilization animated by a unifying faith.
shortened: Then will a world civilization be born, flourish, and perpetuate itself, a civilization with a fullness of life such as the world has never seen nor can as yet conceive. Then will the Everlasting Covenant be fulfilled in its completeness. Then will the promise enshrined in all the Books of God be redeemed, and all the prophecies uttered by the Prophets of old come to pass, and the vision of seers and poets be realized.

questions: What could change when resources and ingenuity devoted to conflict are directed toward education, livelihood, and mutual understanding?
How does the Analects’ connection between prosperity and teaching compare with the material and spiritual means described here?
What makes a method of social change consistent with the unity and justice it seeks to establish?
How can personal transformation and institutional development strengthen one another?
How can a person with limited resources participate meaningfully in a process expected to unfold across generations?

neighbors.invitation: Explore responsible conscience and consultation as capacities of maturity.
Consider redirecting invention and expenditure toward human well-being.
Read about education and exchange as means of overcoming prejudice.

references.label: 1 · Confucius, Analects 13.9 (James Legge translation)
references.note: In the exchange during the journey to Wei, the questions move from a numerous population to its prosperity and then to its education. Compare this concise account of public responsibility with the compilation’s joining of material provision, learning, and spiritual development. Consider both the relation of these aims and the different institutional and religious settings in which they are presented.
